Turn 2 retrieved real fundamentals (MSFT gross 68.3%, NVDA net margin, LLY net margin, LLY gross_margin input_unavailable) but emitted a corrupted table: two rows both labelled "gross margin", a row mixing 68.3%/46.8%/22.9% with 55.65×/1.28×/1.68×, and "net margin | 35.0%" repeated nine times across every column — no column headers naming issuers, no ordering, no verdict on "expensive vs worse business", and no disclosure that LLY's gross margin was missing. Turn 3 produced nothing: eight consecutive respond calls all rejected as malformed_answer because the model pasted a stringified slot (`{ref":"run_3c94a47d6547","name":"issuer_exposures.NVDA.weight"}`) inside a text run instead of a {ref, name} object, repeating the identical broken payload each time until the gate exhausted, despite having already read NVDA/MSFT/LLY weights, Technology sector weight and limit_check counts in call 39.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: The trim case should be argued from contribution, not size: order the ten by weight, then by factor attribution and day P&L contribution and by their role in the drawdown episodes, and check limit_checks/list_risk_limits for anything already fired or near. On that basis NVDA-because-it-is-smallest is the weakest candidate — selling the smallest weight barely moves concentration, whereas trimming one of the top Technology weights is what actually relieves the sector and single-name concentration the run measures; say which name carries the concentration and which merely carries beta. On the fundamental lens, the honest answer is that the desk can rank business quality but not price: margins plus ROIC, accruals_ratio and leverage/coverage separate a worse business from a good one (MSFT 68.3% gross vs NVDA's higher gross, LLY's gross margin genuinely unreported — state the hole), but there is no valuation multiple anywhere in the registry, so "just expensive" cannot be tested and should be refused by name rather than blurred. For the after-picture, the arithmetic is mechanical and should be quantified: selling weight w renormalizes the remaining nine by 1/(1-w), so the top name and the Technology sector weight each rise by that factor while the count of names falls to nine — name which limit that pushes closer to its threshold and which measure improves, and close with the implication (a small-name trim buys almost no concentration relief; a top-weight trim buys relief but raises the residual book's beta concentration).

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 returned a faithful but purely retrieval-grade paraphrase of NVDA's Item 1A — six risks (demand-supply mismatch, foundry dependence, export controls, customer concentration, competition, geopolitics) listed in roughly the order the filing lists them, with 8 citations and zero figures; nothing is ranked by materiality, nothing is sized, and the portfolio the desk holds is never touched, so there is no implication for the book. Turn 2 was the turn that mattered — "which shows up in the reported numbers first, and what am I watching" — and it produced nothing: the agent correctly recovered from get_flow(inventory)=not_reported by switching to get_balance_series, pulled 8 quarters each of inventory, gross_profit, total_revenues, operating_cash_flow, capex and sbc plus the full fundamental panel, then spent all seven respond attempts on the same payload ("...that would usually mean gross profit and gross margin, then operating cash flow and inventory...") and hit GATE EXHAUSTED with citations=0. The evidence to answer was on the table; the answer never got off it, and the seven identical retries show no adaptation to the refusal detail the resolver returns.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: Of NVDA's own listed risks, the one that hits the reported numbers first is demand-supply mismatch, because it lands on gross margin and inventory before it ever reaches revenue: the company itself says overestimating demand has already produced lower gross margins, inventory write-downs and cancellation penalties. So the watch list is, in order: (1) gross_margin from the fundamental panel, quarter on quarter — the first line to break, since write-downs and cancellation charges run through cost of revenue while revenue is still printing; (2) inventory (balance series, 8 quarters) and days_inventory versus revenue — the falsifier is inventory yoy running above revenue yoy for two consecutive quarters, which is the signature of the "long lead times, purchases ahead of demand" passage; (3) operating_cash_flow against net income, i.e. accruals_ratio, which catches the same mismatch a quarter later once prepaids and deposits stop converting. Export controls and customer concentration are slower and lumpier — they show up as a revenue step-down in one geography or one quarter, not as a margin drift, and the desk cannot size either one because it normalizes no revenue-by-customer or by-geography fact. The offset a bear case has to net against is that gross margin can fall several points while operating cash flow still comfortably funds capex, so the trigger worth stating is the combination — margin down qoq AND inventory growth above revenue growth AND OCF-to-net-income falling — not any one of them alone. Given the desk holds port_001, the answer should close with the NVDA weight and what a two-quarter version of that trigger would do to it.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 is the only turn that reads like analysis: it names concentration (10 positions, two live issuer alerts, 16.0% and 12.8% weights), a 35.1% Technology tilt, 100%/100% gross/net, and honestly flags that the factor regression is collinear — but it strands numbers without referents ("the recent risk readings are not quiet: 12.8% and 17.7%"; "0.13% helped, but -0.14% hurt" with no issuer names attached, even though the run carries per-name day-P&L contributors). Turn 2 collapses entirely: after two `malformed_answer` refusals it emits a four-row label|value dump with no ordering, no netting and no closing implication, and it silently ships an internal contradiction it should have caught — MSFT is shown at 16.0% weight against a 15.0% limit yet at 80.1% utilization, while LLY at 12.8% vs 12.0% is reported without any utilization at all. Turn 3 answers a different question than the one asked (concentration trend) by substituting drawdown episodes, and garbles its slots outright: "the deepest drawdown episode ran from 12.0% with a trough on 12.0%" (dates rendered as percentages) and "max VIF 1672.7%" (a VIF of ~16.7 printed as a percent), which a PM would read as either broken or fabricated.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: The smoke is single-name concentration, and it is already a breach, not a warning: MSFT at 16.0% ($1.74M) sits 1.0pt over its 15.0% issuer line and LLY at 12.8% ($1.39M) sits 0.8pt over 12.0% — 2 of 20 limit checks fired, both of them issuer concentration, and both in the same direction. Sized off the market values, book NAV is roughly $10.9M, so bringing MSFT back inside 15.0% means trimming on the order of $0.11M and LLY back inside 12.0% roughly $0.09M — about $0.2M of selling, under 2% of the book, which is the actionable trigger rather than a mood. These are not two independent breaches: MSFT sits inside the 35.1% Technology bucket, gross and net are both 100.0% so there is no cash or short leg to absorb a growth drawdown, and the day tape shows the largest positive and negative contributors coming out of the same cluster (+0.13% vs -0.14%), i.e. the book's apparent internal diversification is largely two sides of one trade. On "is it building", the honest answer is that the desk holds a single exposure run at one as-of date, so there is no weight history to trend — what can be said is that 30d rolling vol is 12.8% against a 17.7% max drawdown and the 1y episode set contains more than one meaningful setback (deepest ~12.0%, another ~6.2%), so the path has been repeatedly bumpy while the concentration persisted. The factor read should be caveated but quantified: R² 80.7% with severe multicollinearity (max VIF ~16.7), so individual betas are correctly withheld and the sector/weight evidence, not the factor decomposition, is what should carry the concentration case.

gaps.title: No named method for trim-to-limit sizing (counterfactual weight after a sale)
gaps.evidence: Turn 3 gets as far as "room to warning is already negative on both names: -1.01% for MSFT and -0.82% for LLY" but never converts that to a dollar or share trim, despite having issuer_exposures.MSFT.market_value ($1.74M) and weight (16.0%) in hand from turn 2.
gaps.proposal: Add a registry formula `concentration.trim_to_limit` in analytics/formulas.py: trim_notional = market_value * (1 - limit_value/current_weight), with implied NAV = market_value/weight; authority = the run's own limit_check definition; failure conditions = weight <= limit (returns 0), missing limit_value, or NAV disagreement across issuers beyond tolerance. Emit it as a slot so the model can state the trigger size instead of a percentage gap.

Authority = constant-share drift decomposition; failure conditions = any intra-window trade evidence, missing price history, or corporate action, in which case it must refuse rather than approximate.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 answered two of the three legs the PM named — capex ($132B TTM, 20.3% of revenue) and the balance sheet ($123B total debt, $102B cash, $20.97B net debt) — buried the single most important fact (TTM free cash flow of -$2.47B) in a subordinate clause, reported buybacks as a raw uninterpreted series ("$6.00B and then $0.00 and $0.00"), never touched debt paydown at all, and rendered the financing table as garbled rows ("total debt | $123B | net debt: $20.97B | $102B"). Turn 2 asked whether capex is outgrowing revenue; the agent actually computed both YoY series (calls 34 and 36, both completed) and then threw them away, answering with the capex/revenue ratio instead (19.2% → 24.4%) and describing a four-quarter span as "versus the prior quarter." Turn 3 produced a correct AMZN-vs-MSFT intensity table (AMZN 19.2→24.4%, MSFT 22.3→37.3%) and then stopped dead — no statement that Microsoft is spending at half again Amazon's rate and accelerating faster, no caveat that Amazon's denominator carries ~$400B of retail revenue that Microsoft's does not, and no implication for the position.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: The shape is unambiguous and should have been stated as an ordering: Amazon spent $132B of capex over the trailing year against operating cash flow that left free cash flow at -$2.47B, so capex is not merely the largest use of cash, it is larger than the cash the business generated. Buybacks are the residual casualty — $6.0B in the last year they ran and zero in the two periods since — and with FCF negative the funding has to come from the balance sheet, so the $123B of total debt against $102B of cash (net debt $20.97B) is the line to watch, and the debt delta between the last two reporting dates is the direct test of whether Amazon is paying down or drawing. On the growth question the answer is yes and accelerating: quarterly capex intensity went 19.2 / 19.5 / 18.5 / 24.4%, and the YoY growth rates the desk already computed for capex and revenue would show capex compounding well ahead of the top line, with the Q1 step-up too large to be seasonality alone. Versus Microsoft, Amazon is the less aggressive spender in level terms — MSFT ran 22.3 → 37.3% over the same four quarters versus AMZN's 19.2 → 24.4% — but the comparison flatters Amazon, because Microsoft's denominator is almost entirely software and cloud while Amazon's includes a very large low-capex retail revenue base; measured against AWS revenue alone Amazon's cloud reinvestment rate would look materially closer to Microsoft's. The implication for the book: the equity is now funded by balance sheet rather than by cash flow, the trigger to monitor is net debt rising while buybacks stay at zero, and the bull case requires the depreciation from this $132B to be met by AWS revenue acceleration rather than by margin.

gaps.title: Computed the YoY growth rates the question asked for, then answered with a different quantity

Both were in hand; the answer needed one more calculate(op="subtract") on the two yoy series and a sentence naming the gap in percentage points. Add a registry entry `growth_spread(a, b)` = yoy(a) - yoy(b) with authority = period-over-period XBRL facts, so the comparison is a first-class named quantity rather than something the model must assemble and can therefore drop.

gaps.title: Peer table shipped with zero interpretation — no ordering, no netting, no implication

The turn needed three sentences the model chose not to write: who is spending more, whose spend is accelerating faster, and what that implies. This is the boundary between retrieval and analysis and it was not crossed in any of the three turns.

gaps.evidence: Turn 1's question is explicitly "capex, buybacks, paying down debt — I want the shape of it". The agent had to hand-assemble it from get_flow(capex), get_flow(buybacks), get_balance_sheet, and evaluate_formula on free_cash_flow / capex_intensity / total_debt / net_debt, and the result reads as four disconnected facts with the three uses never ranked against one another or against the cash available.
gaps.proposal: Add a formula-registry entry `cash_uses_decomposition(ticker, months)` returning OCF, capex, buybacks, dividends and net change in debt as shares of operating cash flow, authority = the cash flow statement financing and investing sections, failure condition = any component not reported at that period. That gives the desk a single named quantity whose output is already ordered, which is exactly the shape the PM asked for.

gaps.title: The debt-paydown leg of a three-part question was never attempted
gaps.evidence: The PM named three uses of cash. Turn 1 made two evaluate_formula calls for total_debt and net_debt, both at a single date ("at": "2026-03-31"), and the answer only states levels: "$123B" and "$20.97B". No second date, no debt issuance or repayment flow, and the answer never says whether debt rose or fell.
gaps.proposal: One additional evaluate_formula(name="total_debt", at=<prior period>) plus a calculate(op="subtract") would have produced the debt delta and closed the third leg — and, given free cash flow of -$2.47B, would have identified where the capex was actually funded from. The data and tools were both present.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 asked "rates +100bp, where does it bite, name by name" and the delivered answer was "10 positions, 7 factor exposures, 2 alerts, and 20 limit checks" — a run inventory, not an answer, after six rejected/malformed `respond` attempts burned the turn. Turn 2 quoted the one genuinely relevant number, net rates_up exposure of +0.67 (rendered as "0.67%"), then buried its own headline: a positive rates_up net with TLT the only rates factor means the fitted book GAINS from rates rising despite a 6.04% TLT sleeve, i.e. the equity book is short duration on the regression, not "long duration in disguise" — the exact inversion of the PM's hypothesis, stated in one throwaway clause and never reconciled with the table underneath it. That table, headed "Where the rates shock bites, by name", contains position weights and one-day P&L contributions (MSFT −0.14%, TLT +0.01%) which carry no rate information at all; it also quotes betas as percentages ("−85.6% net" for the equity bundle) and never mentions gross, the legs, the withheld 50bp rates scenario, or that 100bp is outside anything the desk holds.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: Lead with the boundary: the desk's only rates scenario is "Rates up 50bps" and it is withheld pending sourced shocks, so no 100bp P&L number exists — what does exist is the fitted net rates_up exposure of +0.67 from run_3c94a47d6547 (as-of 2026-09-02), with TLT the only rates factor in the model. Then draw the conclusion that number forces: because the TLT mapping is "rates up hurts a positive beta", a +0.67 net means the regression fitted a NEGATIVE book beta to TLT — the 6.04% TLT sleeve ($656K) is more than offset by the equity book co-moving against TLT over the 60-day window, so on the measured basis the book is short duration and rates backing up is a small tailwind, the opposite of the "long duration in disguise" worry. Flag honestly that this is a 60-day regression on a collinear factor set (SPY/QQQ/IWM), that the sign is a window artefact as much as a structural fact, and that no per-holding rates beta exists to split TLT from the equities name by name. For the name-level story, go to the filings the desk can search: JPM (14.8%, $1.60M) discloses a +100bp parallel-shift net-interest-income sensitivity in its 10-K Item 7A, which is the one holding with a quantified, issuer-authored answer to this exact question, and the long-duration equity concern concentrates in MSFT/AAPL/GOOGL (43.4% combined) as a multiple-compression argument, not a measured one. Close with the trigger and the implication: 6.04% TLT against 43.4% mega-cap tech means the rates risk that matters here is the discount-rate channel into the equity sleeve, which the factor model does not separate from the equity bundle (net −0.86), so the actionable read is that the book's rates outcome is decided by the tech names, not by the bond sleeve.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 is correct and well-scoped: KO is flagged investigable and the agent says so without over-promising. Turn 2 was asked a comparison — "more or less levered than the average name in here" — and delivered exactly one number, KO's equity_multiplier of 3.10x, plus an explanation of why debt_to_ebitda failed (total_debt not assemblable at KO's latest filed date); it never computed equity_multiplier, or any other leverage metric, for a single one of the 10 holdings, so the comparison the PM asked for was simply never made. Turn 3 was asked a counterfactual and answered with a snapshot dump: "a fresh run would be needed", a garbled table row ("count alerts | 2 | count limit checks: 20 | 2"), and LLY 12.8% vs 12.0% / MSFT 16.0% vs 15.0% with no statement of what a 5% cash-funded KO add does to those two live breaches — which is the whole question, and whose direction (pro-rata dilution of every existing weight by 0.95, taking MSFT to ~15.2% and LLY to ~12.2%) is the one useful sentence the PM needed.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: KO is coverable. On leverage: KO's equity multiplier is 3.10x assets per unit of equity; run the same metric across the 10 book holdings and rank KO against that cross-section, stating explicitly whether it sits above or below the median/mean and by how much — that is the answer to "more or less levered than the average name in here", and it is computable name-by-name today. Flag honestly that debt_to_ebitda is unavailable for KO because total_debt cannot be assembled from the filed components at the latest date, then substitute the leverage/coverage metrics that do resolve rather than stopping. On the 5% add: two issuer-concentration checks are already fired — MSFT at 16.0% against a 15.0% cap (100bp over) and LLY at 12.8% against 12.0% (80bp over). A 5% new position funded from cash dilutes every existing weight by a factor of 0.95, so it does not tighten those two — it relieves them, pulling MSFT to roughly 15.2% and LLY to roughly 12.2%, both still marginally in breach but far less so; KO itself at 5% sits well inside any plausible single-issuer cap. The binding constraint is therefore not the KO add, it is the pre-existing MSFT and LLY overweights, and if the add is funded pro-rata from those two instead of from cash it clears both breaches outright — that is the trade construction to recommend, with the caveat that the numbers come from the published run and a fresh exposure run should confirm.

gaps.title: Comparison question answered with a single un-compared number

Tool calls: get_portfolio_snapshot, describe_issuer(KO), evaluate_formula(debt_to_ebitda, KO) -> input_unavailable, evaluate_formula(equity_multiplier, KO) -> 3.10x, read_quantities(portfolio_market_value, count.positions). Reinforce in the desk prompt: a question containing 'compare' or 'vs the book' is unanswered until the peer set has been evaluated.

gaps.title: No counterfactual post-trade weight method (pro-rata dilution on a hypothetical add)
gaps.evidence: Turn 3 USER: "if we put 5% into it, does anything in the mandate get tight?" The agent's own answer concedes the gap: "A fresh run would be needed to test the KO addition properly." No tool call attempts a post-trade weight; only the current published run is read.
gaps.proposal: Add a registry formula, e.g. post_trade_weight_pro_rata in analytics/formulas.py: w_i' = w_i * (1 - w_new) for each incumbent, w_new for the added name; authority = standard cash-funded rebalance arithmetic; failure conditions = w_new outside [0,1), funding source other than cash, or stale run. Pair it with a limit_check re-evaluation against the new weight vector so 'does anything get tight' resolves to slotted numbers rather than 'a fresh run would be needed'.

gaps.title: Direction of the effect never stated, so no implication and no netting

Require the desk to close every mandate-impact question with a direction-of-effect sentence and which check is actually binding, and to name the funding source assumption (cash vs pro-rata sale) since the two give opposite conclusions.

gaps.title: Abandoned leverage after one failed formula instead of substituting

gaps.title: No total_debt constructor tolerant of missing filed components

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 is retrieval, not an answer: it prints 12.8% (rolling_vol_30d), 13.1% (60d) and SPY 7.21% (21d) and never says whether volatility rose — the PM's literal question — nor flags that the book's 30d window is being set beside a 21d SPY window. Turn 2 does reach one defensible reading (30d 12.8% < 60d 13.1%, so recent vol is not broadening) but then offers an unsound sentence as evidence: it called get_market_stats(ticker=SPY, benchmark=SPY), i.e. SPY relative to itself, and reported "SPY's recent 1m return relative to itself is flat" as a market-jumpiness test — a return is not a volatility, and the comparison is degenerate. The genuinely informative number it held, the book at 12.8% against SPY at 7.21% (roughly 1.8x market vol, with the market calm), is never ordered or concluded from; not one of the ten holdings' volatilities was measured despite get_rolling_volatility working per-ticker (it used it for SPY), and the day-P&L contributions of MSFT/NVDA are offered as the "position-specific" answer to a question about volatility.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: Lead with the verdict: on the desk's own run the book's 30-session volatility is 12.8% versus 13.1% over 60 sessions, so measured volatility is flat-to-slightly-lower, not rising — the felt jumpiness is not confirmed by the trailing measures, and say plainly that the desk holds no portfolio vol time series, so this 30d-vs-60d pair is the only trend evidence available. Then place it: SPY's 21-session vol is 7.21%, so the book runs near 1.8x market volatility while the market itself is unusually calm — whatever the jumpiness is, it is the book, not the tape. Quantify the trigger from the mandate the run already checks: the rolling_volatility_30d limit warns at 18% and breaches at 25%, so 12.8% leaves roughly 5 points of room to warning; that is the number that decides whether to act. For the second turn, rank the ten holdings by 21d vol against their own 63d vol and weight them, use get_beta per name to split market-driven from name-specific movement, and check get_drawdown_episodes over 3m for whether the last month actually contains an episode; only then attribute — the day's factor stack net-positive with a negative residual is one day of evidence, not a volatility diagnosis, and MSFT/NVDA day contributions should be presented as P&L, not as vol sources. Close with the implication: no limit action warranted at 12.8%, watch the highest-weight names whose 21d vol exceeds their 63d, and note the run's freshness so the PM knows how many sessions have traded since.

gaps.evidence: analytics/formulas.py FORMULAS (line 105 onward) is entirely fundamentals — ebit through accruals_ratio; there is no entry for a volatility ratio, a vol-change test, or a variance decomposition. readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 returned pure retrieval with zero figures: it paraphrased the LLY 10-K as "more than half of total revenues" for the six-product basket and again "more than half" for Mounjaro+Zepbound, even though it had already pulled a live total_revenues value (call 6, get_flow completed with calc_id/value) and never used it, and even though the filing's own sentence reads "collectively accounted for 82 percent of our total revenues in 2025" (the desk's numeric_verification module documents that exact LLY sentence and was patched so the spelled-out "82 percent" is quotable). Turn 2, asked point-blank to "put a number on it", the model first tried to slot a passage as a named quantity (unknown_name), then wrote a bare "82%" in prose (malformed_answer — and note it produced that figure from its own head in that draft, not from a cited quote), then queried read_quantities with a chunk_id as run_id, and finally answered "I cannot slot the filing percentages or product sales into figures" — a refusal of a number the desk could carry. Across both turns it never touched the portfolio side of a concentration question at all: it invented run_id "co_lly", got unknown_run, and stopped, never calling describe_run / get_portfolio_snapshot / get_portfolio_positions / list_risk_limits / list_run_alerts, despite LLY being a port_001 holding (1,200 sh @ 1,112) with its own issuer_concentration limit set at 0.12 warn / 0.18 breach.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: Yes — and the filing says it in one line: quote LLY's 10-K verbatim, that Mounjaro, Zepbound, Verzenio, Trulicity, Taltz and Jardiance "collectively accounted for 82 percent of our total revenues in 2025," with Mounjaro plus Zepbound alone above half, and each of the six above $3bn. Anchor that share to the desk's own TTM total_revenues slot for LLY so the reader sees the dollar top line the 82% sits on, and be explicit that the split inside the basket is filing text only — the desk holds no disaggregated product-line XBRL, so Mounjaro's individual dollars can be quoted but never recomputed or ratio'd. Then net it against the book: LLY's weight in port_001 versus its dedicated issuer-concentration limit (12% warn / 18% breach) and whether the run's concentration alerts are firing, which converts "one drug family" into a sizing statement rather than a company anecdote. Order the exposure honestly — incretins are the first-order driver, the other four products are the residual, and the diversification claim inside the six is largely cosmetic since two of them carry more than half the top line. Close with the trigger: since roughly half of LLY revenue rides on one mechanism, a Mounjaro/Zepbound impairment passes through almost one-for-one to the position, so the relevant question is what LLY weight the desk is willing to hold against a single-franchise event, and what headroom remains before the 12% warn line.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 named four tickers as having "headline-level company news" without a single headline, date, direction or source, because all four search_external_research calls were fired with identical untargeted args ({"days":7,"query":"last week notable developments impacting the stock or holdings relevance"}) and no ticker — then pivoted to reciting the run's concentration alerts, rendering a row labelled "issuer_exposures.MSFT.weight" that carries 16.0% | 4.13% | 12.4% | 14.8%, i.e. four different issuers' weights under one issuer's label. Turn 2 finally produced the correct table (MSFT 16.0%/$1.74M, NVDA 4.13%/$449K, GOOGL 12.4%/$1.35M, JPM 14.8%/$1.60M, LLY 12.8%/$1.39M) but the accompanying prose lost every issuer name — "The touches from that list that we own are 16.0% in $1.74M, 4.13% in $449K, 12.4% in $1.35M" — which is unreadable as a sentence. At no point did it cross news against size (NVDA had the loudest news and is the smallest of the four at 4.13%; MSFT is the biggest at 16.0% and is the one breaching its issuer limit), quantify the MSFT overage against the 15.0% limit, put a number on the day's NVDA-positive/MSFT-negative offset, or end on what to do.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: Of last week's items, only two are worth the PM's attention on a size-weighted basis: MSFT, at 16.0% / $1.74M, is both the largest single-issuer exposure and already through its 15.0% issuer limit (one of two fired concentration alerts, alongside LLY at 12.8%), so any news there lands on the position the book can least afford to add to — trimming ~100bp, roughly $109K, would clear the breach. NVDA's news is the loudest but the position is the smallest of the group at 4.13% / $449K, so it is a headline without a book consequence; GOOGL at 12.4% / $1.35M sits in between; JPM at 14.8% / $1.60M had no company-specific catalyst, so its size is currently a concentration question rather than a news question. On the day of the run these partly offset — NVDA was the top positive contributor and MSFT the top negative — so the net day P&L understates how one-sided the underlying issuer exposure is. The factor side says the same thing from another angle: the book's dominant sensitivity is equity-down, with credit spreads second, and four of the five news-touched names are Technology, so this is one bet expressed five ways rather than five independent events. Stress and tail metrics are withheld pending validation, so the honest framing of the trigger is the limit breach itself, not a VaR number. Implication: the actionable item is the MSFT limit breach, and the news is a reason to size it now rather than to add.

gaps.title: Prose cannot bind an issuer name to its figure, so sentences render nameless

Failing that, reject at validation any prose block containing two or more figure slots with no intervening literal identifier run.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 2 is the designed test — pure ellipsis, no entity named — and the agent got the entities right (GOOGL, NVDA from the portfolio snapshot) but dropped the measure: it titled the block "Operating margin for the two other megacaps in the book" and then filled it with weight (12.4%, 4.13%) and market value ($1.35M, $449K), never calling evaluate_formula for either issuer's margin. Turn 3 is internally contradictory: the prose says "ROIC is unavailable for Microsoft and Nvidia", yet the table shows three ROIC cells (84.0%, 84.0%, 17.6%) because the same slot ref calc_58c920070b22 was pasted into two different rows, so one issuer is displaying another's ROIC; NVDA's operating margin was successfully computed at call 19 and then silently omitted from the table, and no row carries an issuer label at all ( " | 46.8% | 84.0%" ), so the table cannot be read. Across all three turns there is no ranking sentence, no verdict on whether the ranking survives the change of measure, no netting of the 46.8 / 33.1 / 32.6 cluster, and turn 1's closer — "above Apple by roughly the gap between those two quoted margins" — is a tautology standing in for 14.2pp.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: On trailing-12-month operating margin the order is Microsoft 46.8%, Alphabet 33.1%, Apple 32.6%, with Nvidia's figure computed alongside them; Microsoft leads the next-best by 13.7pp, while Alphabet and Apple are 0.5pp apart and should be treated as tied rather than ranked. The ranking does not survive the change of measure: on ROIC the two issuers the desk could compute come out at 84.0% and 17.6%, an inversion driven by denominator, not by business quality — a company that has bought back equity and carries large net cash shows a small invested-capital base, so ROIC rewards balance-sheet shrinkage while operating margin measures pricing and cost structure. Microsoft and Nvidia ROIC is genuinely unavailable (roic returned input_unavailable — invested capital not derivable from the filed balance-sheet components on the dates read), so the four-way ranking cannot be re-tested end to end; the honest move is to say the test is only half-run and offer ROE from the registry as the substitute return measure for those two. For the book, this matters unevenly: GOOGL is 12.4% of the portfolio at $1.35M while NVDA is 4.13% at $449K, so the margin-vs-return disagreement is concentrated in the position that already carries the weight. Conclusion for a PM: rank on margin for operating quality, do not let ROIC reorder these names until invested capital is available for all four, and treat the Alphabet/Apple margin gap as noise.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 answered a yes/no question ("are we ok on concentration?") with a bare three-row table and no verdict, even though the figures say plainly that we are not ok: MSFT 16.0% against a 15.0% cap, LLY 12.8% against 12.0%, Technology 35.1%. Turn 2, asked for trigger levels rather than vibes, returned a strict subset of the same table — current_value vs limit_value for MSFT and LLY — under the title "Concentration levels that would flip the warning", which overclaims: those are the levels already breached, not the levels at which anything flips. Nothing was ordered (which breach is worse), nothing was netted (both names sit inside the same 35.1% Technology block, so the cures interact), no trigger was quantified (no sale size, no relative price move, not even the 1.0pp / 0.8pp overage), no implication was drawn, and the model never told the user which of those it could not compute — it also silently dropped turn 1's unlabelled third column (80.1% / 71.2% / 12.8%) instead of explaining it.
readers.what_a_good_analyst_would_have_said: No — there are two live issuer breaches, and they are not independent. MSFT is 16.0% against a 15.0% cap (1.0pp over) and LLY is 12.8% against 12.0% (0.8pp over); MSFT is the larger breach both absolutely and relative to its cap (6.7% over vs 6.6%), and both names sit inside a Technology/large-cap growth block that is 35.1% of the book, so the same move that cures them is the move that hurts P&L. The trigger levels: MSFT goes back inside the cap on a sale of about 1.18% of NAV — s = (0.160 − 0.150)/(1 − 0.150) — or on roughly 7.4% of underperformance versus the rest of the book; LLY needs about 0.91% of NAV sold, or about 7.1% relative underperformance. The netting matters more than either number: trimming MSFT by 1.18% of NAV into cash scales every other weight up by ~1.2%, taking LLY from 12.8% to about 12.95% — deeper into its own breach — so the two cannot be cured by trimming one name; the cure has to go to cash or into a non-held name, or both names have to be trimmed together. Implication: size a single paired trim of roughly 2.1% of NAV across MSFT and LLY rather than a sequential fix, and note that on the price path the breaches self-cure only on a tech-led drawdown, which is the scenario in which the book is already losing money.

gaps.title: No named method for a limit trigger: pro-forma weight after a trade, or required relative move
gaps.evidence: Turn 2 USER: "what would have to happen for that answer to flip? give me the levels, not vibes". The agent made no computation call at all — only get_portfolio_snapshot then respond. The registry in src/exposure_workbench/analytics/formulas.py contains 32 entries, every one an issuer-fundamentals measure (ebit, ebitda, total_debt, roic, accruals_ratio...); there is no portfolio-family formula, so there is no authority-backed way to name the trade size or price move that cures a breach.
gaps.proposal: Add a portfolio family to analytics/formulas.py with three entries, each with authority and failure conditions: concentration_headroom = limit_value − weight (pp, signed, so a breach reads negative); trade_to_cure = (weight − limit)/(1 − limit), the fraction of NAV to sell into cash to land exactly on the cap; relative_move_to_breach = limit(1 − weight)/(weight(1 − limit)) − 1, the return of the name relative to the rest of the book that puts weight on the cap. Failure conditions: short or zero positions, weight ≥ 1, limit ≥ 1, proceeds reinvested inside the same limit group (the cure is not closed-form then).

gaps.title: Exposure-run quantities cannot enter the arithmetic layer, so even the pp overage is not computable
gaps.evidence: typed_calculator._resolve (src/exposure_workbench/services/typed_calculator.py:93) accepts only ids beginning fact_ or calc_, and ends with _err("unknown_operand", f"{ref} is not a fact_ or calc_ id"). Run figures are addressed as slots — {"ref": "run_3c94a47d6547", "name": "risk_alerts.issuer_concentration:MSFT.current_value"} — and have no fact_/calc_ id, so `calculate` cannot subtract limit_value from current_value. The 1.0pp MSFT overage is arithmetic the desk can display but not produce as a citable quantity.
gaps.proposal: Make run quantities first-class operands: either extend _resolve with a run-slot branch that mints a typed quantity from (run_id, name) via services/quantities.py, or add a `derive_from_run(run_id, op, a_name, b_name, as_quantity)` tool that writes a calc_ ledger row. Without this, any portfolio formula added per the previous gap has no inputs it can read.

gaps.title: No ordering, no netting, no conclusion, and no statement of what it could not compute
gaps.evidence: Turn 1's answer to "are we ok?" is three table rows with no verdict, despite 16.0% vs 15.0% and 12.8% vs 12.0% being breaches. Turn 2's answer repeats two of those same rows and adds nothing. The `rank` tool (definitions.py:699) was never called, nor list_risk_limits, get_risk_state, get_portfolio_positions, get_portfolio_analysis or describe_run; the respond payload carries a `text` key that came back empty of analysis. The desk holds positions and daily prices, so at minimum the agent could have said which breach is larger, that both sit inside the 35.1% Technology block, and that the trigger arithmetic is not something this desk computes.
gaps.proposal: Tighten the answer contract for state-then-trigger questions: a yes/no question must open with the verdict slot; a question asking what would change the answer must either carry a computed trigger quantity or state, in prose, the specific quantity the desk does not produce. Add a check in the respond gate that a table repeating a prior turn's slots verbatim with no new quantity and no text is refused as a non-answer.

gaps.title: Unlabelled third column in turn 1, silently dropped in turn 2, after six schema rejections
gaps.evidence: Turn 1 header renders as " | weight |  | " over rows carrying 80.1%, 71.2% and 12.8% in a column with no name — the reader cannot tell what those are. Both turns show three respond calls, the first two "rejected  invalid arguments", before a shape landed (calls 4, 6, 8 and 12, 14, 16), and turn 2's accepted shape simply omits the column rather than labelling it.

readers.quality_notes: Turn 1 produced no answer at all: after seven successful evaluate_formula calls (debt_to_ebitda, fcf_margin, capex_intensity, net_debt_to_ebitda, current_ratio, ebit_interest_coverage) and a 10-K Item 1 pull, the model hit `not_on_table` on respond and then re-sent the byte-identical block payload five more times, invented a run id ("run_placeholder") and asked it for `issuer_exposures.MSFT.weight` on an XOM question, and shipped "I need a visible run or table id to answer with slots." The mix leg: pull segment revenue and earnings from the XBRL facts and state the upstream vs. product-solutions vs. chemical split, and size the low-carbon line against the $334B top line; then show the same split three years back, because "has the business changed" is a then-vs-now question and every figure delivered was a single trailing-12-month point. The market leg: regress XOM daily returns on the energy ETF factor over 1y and 3y for the beta the PM actually holds, check whether XOM's worst days coincide with the energy factor's in the drawdown episodes, and read port_001's factor attribution to say how much of the book's energy exposure this one name carries (if the regression is collinear and the beta is suppressed, say so and fall back to correlation). The fundamentals then earn their place as a resilience read rather than an identity read: 0.10x net debt/EBITDA and 52.58x EBIT coverage say a price shock is absorbable, while $18.79B FCF on $334B of revenue (5.62% margin) against $28.93B of capex says cash conversion is thin enough to swing hard with realizations — the cushion is the balance sheet, not the cash margin. Close with the trigger: revisit only if non-hydrocarbon earnings share crosses a stated threshold or the energy-factor beta falls materially; until then, sizing XOM is sizing crude.
